outline.title: Intro to C Programming
outline.description: An entry‑level course that introduces the fundamentals of the C programming language, covering syntax, data types, control structures, and basic I/O. Designed for beginners with no prior programming experience.
objectives: Understand the role and importance of the C language in software development
Write simple C programs using variables, data types, and operators
Apply control structures such as loops and conditionals to solve problems
Perform input and output operations with the standard library
Compile and run C code using a common compiler

lessons.title: Getting Started with C
learning_objectives: Identify the components of a basic C program
Explain the role of the compiler and linker
Recognize the syntax of main function and comments
Understand the difference between header files and source files
lessons.summary: This lesson introduces the C language ecosystem, covering how source code is compiled and linked into an executable. Students will write, compile, and run a simple "Hello, World!" program, learning essential tools and syntax.

lessons.title: Variables, Data Types, and Operators
learning_objectives: Define and declare variables of various primitive types
Use integer, floating-point, and character data types
Apply arithmetic, logical, and relational operators
Understand type promotion and conversion rules
lessons.summary: Students will explore C's data model, learning how to store and manipulate values. Hands‑on exercises include calculating areas, converting units, and evaluating expressions.

lessons.title: Control Flow and I/O
learning_objectives: Create loops (for, while, do‑while) to repeat actions
Read user input and display output using printf and scanf
Handle basic error checking in input
lessons.summary: The final lesson equips learners to build interactive programs. By combining control flow with I/O, students will solve practical problems such as a simple calculator and a number‑guessing game.

1.title: Getting Started with C
1.introduction: Welcome to the first step in learning the C programming language! In this lesson we’ll cover the essential building blocks of a C program, from its basic structure to the tools that turn your code into a running application. By the end, you’ll know how a compiler and linker work together, what the main function looks like, and the difference between header and source files.

sections.heading: The Anatomy of a C Program
sections.explanation: A minimal C program is made of a header inclusion, the main function, and optionally comments that explain the code. This section shows the exact syntax and shows how the compiler expects the program to be structured.

sections.heading: Compiling and Linking
sections.explanation: When you write C code, a compiler translates it into machine code. The linker then combines multiple object files and libraries into a single executable. Understanding these steps helps you troubleshoot build errors and manage large projects.
sections.example:
gcc -c hello.c   # compile to object file hello.o
ld hello.o -o hello   # link to create executable
./hello              # run the program

sections.heading: Header vs. Source Files
sections.explanation: Header files (.h) declare interfaces, while source files (.c) contain implementations. The compiler processes source files, and the linker resolves references using header declarations and object files.

1.summary: You now understand the core components of a C program, how compilers and linkers turn source code into an executable, and the clear separation between header and source files. With these fundamentals, you’re ready to write, compile, and organize your own C projects.

exercises.task: Write a simple C program that prints "Learning C is fun!" and explain why each line is necessary.
exercises.hint: Remember to include the proper header and define the main function with the correct return type.

exercises.task: Create a header file "utils.h" with a function prototype for "int multiply(int, int);" and a source file "utils.c" that implements this function. Then write a main program that uses it.
exercises.hint: Use include guards in the header and make sure the source file includes the header you just wrote.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the minimal structure of a C program?
questions.explanation: The minimal C program requires a header inclusion for I/O, a main function with the signature int main(void), and a return statement. This exact syntax matches the example in the lesson.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the compiler in the C build process?
options: It links object files into an executable.
It translates C source code into machine code object files.
It runs the compiled program on the target machine.
It manages memory allocation during program execution.
questions.correct_answer: It translates C source code into machine code object files.
questions.explanation: The compiler converts source (.c) files into object (.o) files. The linker then combines these objects into an executable.

questions.question: Which command sequence correctly compiles and runs a C program named hello.c?
options:
gcc hello.c -c -o hello.o
ld hello.o -o hello
./hello
questions.explanation: First, gcc with -c compiles to an object file hello.o; then ld links that object into hello; finally ./hello runs it.

questions.question: In the context of C files, what is the main difference between a header (.h) and a source (.c) file?
options: Header files contain implementation code, source files contain only declarations.
Source files are compiled directly, while header files are only included by source files.
Header files declare interfaces; source files contain implementations.
Source files are compiled after header files, which are never linked.
questions.correct_answer: Header files declare interfaces; source files contain implementations.
questions.explanation: Headers provide function prototypes and definitions needed by the compiler; sources provide the actual function bodies compiled into object files.

questions.question: Why should a header file include an include guard like #ifndef/#define/#endif?
options: To prevent the header from being compiled twice by the compiler.
To ensure the header is linked after all source files.
To allow the compiler to ignore the header if it contains errors.
To enforce that only one source file includes the header.
questions.correct_answer: To prevent the header from being compiled twice by the compiler.
questions.explanation: Include guards stop multiple inclusion of the same header, avoiding redefinition errors during compilation.
